EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN ─ NEW JERSEY MINIMUM-WAGE INCREASE, APRIL 1992  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Two–way-fixed-effects Difference-in-Differences (DID), supplemented with an event-study specification.

Why appropriate
• Sharp policy change confined to one state (NJ) at a known date (1 Apr 1992).  
• Adjacent Pennsylvania (PA) provides a natural untreated comparison group that shares the same federal floor, macro environment, industrial mix, and seasonality.  
• Restaurant-level panel observed pre- and post-treatment, allowing us to difference out time-invariant restaurant heterogeneity and common shocks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 if restaurant located in New Jersey, 0 if in eastern Pennsylvania.

Control group  
Fast-food outlets (same four chains) in eastern PA zip codes included in the sampling frame.

Treatment timing  
Post = 1 for observations whose pay period end-date ≥ 1 April 1992; 0 for pay periods finishing before that date. (With two observation windows this simplifies to Feb–Mar 1992 vs Nov–Dec 1992.)

Running variable & cutoff  
Not applicable (no RDD).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel-trends: Absent the NJ increase, employment in NJ and PA restaurants would have evolved in parallel.  
Plausibility: Both states were on the same federal minimum through 3/92; the sample is geographically contiguous (eastern PA) and limited to identical chains. We will test pre-trends with longer-horizon BLS data and chain-level administrative files.

A2. No differential contemporaneous shocks: Nothing else hits NJ fast-food market differently from PA over Apr–Dec 1992.  
Plausibility: No other labor or tax legislation specific to NJ fast food in 1992 is known. Nonetheless, we will control for county-level unemployment and personal-income growth.

A3. Stable composition / no selective attrition: Treatment shouldn’t induce exit or differential reporting that biases measured employment.  
Plausibility: Same administrative payroll vendor covers both states; we will check balanced-panel results and include a 0-employment cell for permanent closures.

A4. SUTVA / no cross-border spillovers: PA restaurants do not adjust employment because of NJ’s higher wage.  
Plausibility: Some cross-border commuting exists, but most fast-food jobs are local and lowskilled; nonetheless, we will test robustness dropping PA counties that border NJ.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Divergent pre-trends  
Fix: Graph and regress longer-period event-study coefficients using ES-202/BLS-790 series 1982–1996. Fail-safe: include chain-by-county linear time trends.

T2. Selective sample attrition (NJ closings)  
Fix: Create an “employment including zeros” balanced panel; run Lee-bounds on exit; show comparable closure rates.

T3. Spillovers / commuting contamination  
Fix: Restrict control group to PA zip codes > 25 miles from NJ border; test sensitivity of β under varying radii.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
############################################################
# 0. Packages
############################################################
library(data.table)     # fast data handling
library(fixest)         # two–way FE regressions
library(modelsummary)   # nice tables
library(ggplot2)

############################################################
# 1. Load & merge data
############################################################
# assumes two csvs: payroll_pre.csv, payroll_post.csv
pre  <- fread("payroll_pre.csv")   # Feb–Mar 92
post <- fread("payroll_post.csv")  # Nov–Dec 92
dat  <- rbindlist(list(pre, post), use.names = TRUE)

############################################################
# 2. Variable construction
############################################################
dat[, treat  := ifelse(state == "NJ", 1, 0)]            # NJ=1
dat[, post   := ifelse(period == "post", 1, 0)]         # Nov–Dec=1
dat[, did    := treat*post]                             # interaction
dat[, fteemp := payroll_hours / 35 ]                    # outcome

# optional: create balanced panel id
setkey(dat, restaurant_id, period)
bal <- dat[, .N, by = restaurant_id][N == 2]$restaurant_id
dat[, balanced := restaurant_id %in% bal]

############################################################
# 3. Main DID specification
############################################################
# Two–way FE, clustering at zip-code level
did_main <- feols(fteemp ~ treat*post | restaurant_id + period,
                  cluster = 'zipcode', data = dat)
etable(did_main)

############################################################
# 4. Robustness: drop PA border counties
############################################################
dat_rb <- dat[border25 == 0]     # assume pre-coded indicator
did_rb <- feols(fteemp ~ treat*post | restaurant_id + period,
                cluster = 'zipcode', data = dat_rb)
etable(list(Main = did_main, DropBorder = did_rb))

############################################################
# 5. Event study on quarterly BLS county data
############################################################
bls <- fread("bls_county_qtr.csv")   # county-quarter panel 1988-1995
bls[, treat := ifelse(state == "NJ", 1, 0)]
bls[, rel_qtr := quarter - 1992.25]  # 1992Q2 = 0 (April–June)
# create dummies for each relative quarter k ≠ −1 baseline
for(k in -8:8){
  if(k != -1){
    bls[, paste0("D",k) := (rel_qtr == k)]
  }
}
rhs <- paste(paste0("D", setdiff(-8:8, -1)), collapse = " + ")
fs   <- as.formula(paste("log(emp_fastfood) ~", rhs, "| county + quarter"))
ev   <- feols(fs, data = bls, cluster = "county")
iplot(ev) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Neoclassical labor demand predicts β < 0: a higher binding wage should lower employment. Elasticity estimates in the literature cluster between −0.1 and −0.3 for low-wage industries. The NJ hike (≈19 %) would thus be expected to cut employment by roughly 2–5 % (≈0.05–0.15 FTE per store on a mean of ~8 FTE).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Common-trend pre-period verified graphically ...................... 0.8  
C2: No simultaneous confounding policy shocks ........................ 0.7  
C3: Stable sample / no differential attrition ........................ 0.7  
C4: No spillovers or interference (SUTVA) ............................ 0.6  
C5: Reliable outcome measurement & same definition across groups ..... 0.9  

Average score = 0.74 → research design reasonably credible but relies on checking pre-trends and ruling out subtle spillovers.
